title: Bill Gates warns the 'evolutionary' age of AI will be brutal for workers
content:
People are going to keep on losing their jobs to AI because “the incentive structure [in business] is wrong: It’s ‘hire the robot, fire the human and don’t look back’,” Bill Gates tells The Observer in an exclusive interview.
Describing the AI age as an “evolutionary event” where humans are no longer the most intelligent things on the planet, he forecasts wholesale disruption to the labour market as almost all work skills – “skills of invention, skills of white-collar work and then with humanoids, the skills of physical human labour” – are replaced by AI.
Governments will need to find new sources of income to fund the needs of people put out of work, future education and re-skilling: “The revenue for the safety net to help us through this transition will actually be reduced, even though overall prosperity gets better.” He wants to see taxes on AI use, perhaps in the form of a “token tax”.
He also says that billionaires should pay more tax. He says he would have been willing to pay “a little more than double” the tax he has paid – he has paid $14bn in tax in his lifetime, but would have been willing to pay $40bn. “Governments [need to] figure out how to tax very wealthy people in a way that feels fair. It doesn’t solve the fact that government spending versus government tax collection in many rich countries, including the US, is out of whack… that disparity’s gotten larger in the last few years. So at some point, more taxes will have to be raised, and some spending will have to be curbed.”
While keen to stress the “good stuff” that could be enabled by AI, such as enhanced drug discovery, Gates warned that technological advances will present a “real test of quality of government”, at a time when developed countries are already fire-fighting on multiple fronts and geopolitical tensions are high. “You could say this isn’t the best time to say, hey, rich countries, let’s do the hardest thing you’ve ever done,” he said.
The philanthropist and Microsoft founder highlighted bioterrorism and cyberattacks as the most pressing short-term threats, but that, by the end of the 2020s, artificial intelligence could be operating beyond human control. Within three to four years, he says, “you hope that you’ve gotten very serious about the alignment control issues”, i.e. the risk of AIs operating in ways that no longer align with human interests.
The UK is perhaps better placed than most: its regulatory framework and state capacity on AI have been praised internationally and by industry insiders. Ahead of a budget that is expected to stress the importance of “resilience”, the chancellor made a flurry of AI-related spending announcements aiming to build on this strong start. There were two major themes: protecting Britain against emerging threats – including those highlighted by Gates – and promoting domestic innovation to avoid reliance on technologies developed overseas.
The US and China will, on a few of these issues, have to view [AI] as a challenge to humanity, not a nation-state win-lose type situation
Bill Gates
The government yesterday announced £100m of funding for a new AI Biosecurity Lab, the world’s first, with responsibility for monitoring biological threats and developing medical countermeasures. The lab will be supported by up to £200m of model credits from Anthropic and OpenAI.
The AI Security Institute, the UK’s internationally admired agency responsible for testing the capabilities of AI models, will receive a further £120m of funding. An additional £60m will go towards a National Cyber Shield, £70m towards a new National Exposure and Real-Time Vulnerability (Nerv) Centre, and £23m towards the government’s new AI Economics Institute, which is chaired by Nobel prize winner Simon Johnson and tasked with analysing the emerging economic impacts of AI.
In keeping with the government’s interventionist inclinations, and its willingness to use the public sector balance sheet to “pick winners”, the UK’s Sovereign AI fund has also been backed with £120m of new funding, an increase of around 25%. Half will go towards direct investments in promising UK AI companies, and half towards an R&D procurement scheme, to foster innovative solutions in areas like cybersecurity and healthcare.
Kanishka Narayan, the minister for AI, has spoken repeatedly of the importance of the UK having strategic leverage over AI technology. That wouldn’t mean the UK duplicating all parts of the AI supply chain, but instead the pursuit of a small number of globally leading capabilities that other countries would struggle to manage without. A non-exclusive set of candidates include a global role for the AI Security Institute in safety evaluations, domestic computing capacity and expertise in chip design.
So-called “middle powers” like the UK are trying to pick a path through a world dominated by two AI superpowers. Gates warned in his interview that co-operation between those superpowers will be required to avert the AI-related risks that are causing so much worry inside the leading labs. “The US and China will, on a few of these issues, have to view it as a challenge to humanity, not a nation-state win-lose type situation.” he said.
Gates also spoke to The Observer of his regret over his links with the paedophile financier Jeffrey Epstein, which were the subject of a US Congressional committee hearing in June. “It definitely was a damaging thing to have spent time with him,” he said, adding that he has “lots of things where I look back and I say, okay, I hope what I learned from that is better than whatever pain or problems that it caused”.
Photograph by Getty Images

report.summary: Bill Gates says AI will displace most human labor, and governments must tax AI use and extreme wealth to fund the transition.
report.background: Gates has been publicly optimistic about AI's benefits — drug discovery, education, productivity — while warning about labor disruption since at least 2017, when he proposed taxing robots that replace human workers. The 'token tax' is the same logic applied to generative AI, where usage is metered in tokens. The interview lands amid a shift in the debate: early ChatGPT-era framing treated AI as a 'copilot' that augments workers, but agentic systems and humanoid robot programs have pushed executives and economists toward openly discussing substitution. Simultaneously, governments are being asked to fund safety infrastructure — model evaluations, biosecurity monitoring, cyber defense — while their tax bases still depend on human labor. The UK has positioned itself as a 'middle power' with outsized influence on AI safety testing, and its budget announcements attempt to convert regulatory reputation into industrial strategy.
key_points: Gates argues the problem is not AI's limits but business incentives: 'hire the robot, fire the human and don't look back.' Even if AI only matches human performance, the economics favor replacement, so displacement will continue regardless of how carefully companies talk about augmentation. Policy, not technical progress, is the lever he sees.

His list of vulnerable skills is unusually broad: invention, white-collar work, and — once humanoid robots mature — physical labor. That implies near-total coverage of the labor market rather than a shock confined to one segment, which is why he calls it an 'evolutionary event' in which humans are no longer the most intelligent things on the planet.

The fiscal trap: as labor's share of income shrinks, payroll and income tax receipts shrink with it, precisely when spending on safety nets and reskilling must rise. Gates says safety-net revenue 'will actually be reduced, even though overall prosperity gets better,' and proposes taxes on AI use — possibly a 'token tax' on metered model usage — plus higher taxes on billionaires.

He says he has paid $14bn in tax over his lifetime but would have accepted $40bn, 'a little more than double.' He frames the wider issue as structural: in rich countries including the US, spending and tax collection are 'out of whack,' so eventually taxes must rise and some spending be curbed.

On risk, bioterrorism and cyberattacks are the near-term threats; by the end of the decade alignment and control failures could put AI beyond human control, making the next three to four years the window. The UK budget answers with £100m for a first AI Biosecurity Lab, £120m more for the AI Security Institute, £60m for a National Cyber Shield, £70m for a vulnerability centre, £23m for an AI Economics Institute and £120m more for its Sovereign AI fund.
report.impact: For the AI industry, Gates's framing shifts the argument from capability to distribution: expect more scrutiny of per-token pricing as a taxable meter, and pressure on labs to fund evaluation and biosecurity infrastructure — Anthropic and OpenAI are already contributing model credits in the UK. For developers, the practical signal is that evaluation, safety engineering, red-teaming and AI-security work are becoming funded, government-backed career paths, while routine implementation work faces the same substitution pressure Gates describes. For regular users, the near-term experience is likely more job insecurity before any dividend arrives: better tools and rising productivity, plus tax debates that determine whether displaced workers get re-skilling support. Notably, none of the policies Gates favors — token taxes, wealth taxes, alignment deadlines — are close to implementation.
report.tools: Watch the UK AI Security Institute's Inspect framework, an open-source library for building and running model evaluations; EleutherAI's lm-evaluation-harness for benchmarking; and METR's task-based agent evaluations. The newly funded AI Economics Institute, chaired by Nobel laureate Simon Johnson, will publish on labor-market impacts. For biosecurity, track the announced AI Biosecurity Lab and its Anthropic/OpenAI model credits. The 'token tax' debate is best followed through national tax-policy consultations.
